title: `I loved Frank ... that was not Frank': Husband's murderous rage shocks his widow
article: Sally McIntyre woke up Wednesday morning to find a man she didn't know.
Her gentle, loving husband, Frank Hutterer, had changed badly, for no apparent reason.

As she prepared her eight-year-old son Benjamin for school, Mr. Hutterer, apparently possessed by a strange dark rage, confronted her and began screaming. Benjamin looked on, wondering when his dad would stop yelling and walk him to school as he did every day.
Confused and surprised, Ms. McIntyre yelled back and tried to calm him. But his rage grew hotter and his manner became violent.
And for the first time in their 11-year marriage, Ms. McIntyre, 34, a prominent women's rights advocate, feared her husband.

In tears, she pulled Benjamin aside and whispered: "Ben, you're going to have to be a big boy today. You're going to have to walk to school by yourself. I need you to be a big, strong boy. Go right now. Please go."

She gently, urgently pushed him out the door of their Stittsville home and the boy began walking to school alone for the first time in his life, looking over his shoulder the whole way, trying to understand what was happening.

In the moments that followed their only child's departure, around 8:45 a.m. Wednesday, Mr. Hutterer, 35, grabbed two butcher knives and attacked his wife. She managed to break free and scramble across Cordukes Street to the home of their elderly neighbours, Mitch Smith, 71, and his wife Margaret, 69.
As if possessed by an evil spirit, Mr. Hutterer followed her, chanting repeatedly in a high-pitched voice, "You are dead! You are dead!"
Mr. Hutterer cornered his wife at the door in the Smiths' carport.
With a butcher knife in each hand, he began stabbing her repeatedly in jerky, robot-like motions, the chilling death chant never ceasing. The Smiths tried to stop him and he stabbed them, too.

Then, leaving his wife lying motionless on the Smiths' driveway, blood pouring from her wounds and her mouth, Mr. Hutterer walked down to the road to meet the Ottawa-Carleton police officer who had just arrived. He adjusted his chant, now screeching, "You are dead! I am dead!"
And then he was.

The female police officer pleaded with him to drop his knives. He lunged at her and she shot him once, but it had little effect. He continued at her and she shot him three more times, in rapid succession, and he dropped dead.

Two of Mr. Hutterer's four brothers, Brian and Mark Hutterer, made the long drive from Alliston, Ont., yesterday to visit Ms. McIntyre at the Ottawa Hospital's Civic site, where she was in fair condition. Through their shock, they felt nervous about how she would receive them. When they approached her bed, she smiled, and they all wept together.
"I loved Frank," she told them. "I love him still. Frank did not do this. That was not Frank."

Born in Caledon, Ont., Mr. Hutterer moved with his parents and brothers to a farm in the town of Alliston, north of Toronto, as a teenager. He excelled at school, wrestling and football and anything else he tackled.
He met Ms. McIntyre when he was studying graphic design at Carleton University. They fell in love and married 11 years ago.
With their baby boy, they moved to the quiet bungalow on Cordukes Street in Stittsville several years ago. They would become well- known and liked by all their neighbours.

While Ms. McIntyre worked as an environmental planner at the engineering firm R.V. Anderson, Mr. Hutterer stayed home to take care of Benjamin. He spent much of his time restoring what had been a rundown bungalow.

In the leisure time they shared, Mr. Hutterer, Ms. McIntyre and Ben would hike, bike, canoe and skate together and make frequent visits to the Hutterer family homestead in Alliston. They were expected there this weekend for Thanksgiving dinner.

Mr. Hutterer's oldest brother, Dave, had called on Sunday to confirm the visit. Nothing seemed awry, other than Ms. McIntyre's back spasms, likely brought on by the gardening she had done with her husband last weekend.

"It didn't matter what season it was," brother Mark Hutterer said. "They'd just enjoy it together. They were just a perfect happy family. He was a very devoted father and loving husband and he became a friend to anyone he met. She is the sister we never had. They were always so in love."

An astronomy enthusiast, Mr. Hutterer taught his son about the planets and the stars. Skilled in carpentry and electrical work, he recently renovated the home by himself. He even made his own automatic garage door openers.
She was the former head of the National Action Committee on the Status of Women in Eastern Ontario and frequently spoke out against and wrote on violence against women.
"He could do anything," said Brian Hutterer. "He could take on any project. And he was a soft-spoken gentleman on top of that."
"No one knows what happened," Brian said. "I guess we'll never know. That wasn't Frank. He simply was not like that. This is like a bad dream and I want to snap my fingers and wake up, but I can't."
Their thoughts then shifted to the police officer who killed their brother.
"I hope the police officer is OK," Mark said. "I'm sure it wasn't her intention to wake up and kill somebody that day. She was doing her job."
Mr. Hutterer had told neighbours he had surgery on his brain about four years ago.
The province's Special Investigations Unit is handling the case.
